newsitem.title: FRANCE: Hefty rise in Burgundy prices expected.
newsitem.headline: Hefty rise in Burgundy prices expected.

text.p: Burgundy wine professionals forecast a hefty price increase at this year's annual Hospices de Beaune charity auction, boosted by high yields and excellent quality of the 1996 vintage.
Several trade specialists and journalists predicted increases of 10 to 25 percent.
The Hospices will sell 607 casks of red and 112 of white wine on Sunday afternoon at its annual charity auction, a 27 percent increase compared to last year.
The auction is closely watched around the world as an early indicator of the direction of wine prices and the overall health of France's crucial wine trade.
The wine-drinking public will get its first chance to sample this year's vintage on Thursday, when bottles of Beaujuolais Nouveau are uncorked around the world amid traditional hype and festivities.
The Beaujolais is flown around the world in time for ceremonial uncorking at one minute past midnight on Wednesday.

Burgundy wine trade officials said they hoped any price increase at this year's sale would be modest, but professionals and journalists said that because of the quality of the vintage, it might be hard to limit buyers' enthusiasm.
"Nobody wants prices to go up and nobody wants prices to go down," said Burgundy Wine Board president Louis Trebuchet, striking a note of caution at an official luncheon on Saturday.
"We want a better link between quality and price. If we are reasonable, Burgundy will be able to take care of itself," he said.
Trebuchet said Burgundy's international reputation for sky-high prices and spotty quality could be improved if prices proved less volatile in the years ahead.

"We need to establish a reputation of predictability for the consumer," he told Reuters. "What has been held against Burgundy is not just that its wines are too expensive, it's their unpredictability."
Most agreed that cool, wet conditions in July and August combined with excellent weather during the harvest season will have produced wines with the greatest potential for some time.
"It's the best year since 1990," said one trade journalist with 15 years' experience tasting the young wine out of huge oak barrels -- a tricky business for the unschooled.
Trebuchet was more expansive, saying he believed the region had not produced such quantity with such consistent quality since 1959.

Average yields this year were about 30 percent higher this year than in 1995. But despite the increase, alcohol and acidity levels are high, color robust and tannins evident, indicating good potential for aging, professionals said.
Officials from the Hospices winery were careful to say that the increase in yields was not due to lax quality control.
During grape sorting before vinification, only three to five percent of the grapes had to be eliminated because of rot or lack of ripeness, said Andre Jacquet, president of the Hospices.
Last year up to a third of the harvest had to be thrown away to maintain quality.

Proceeds from the auction after production costs go to the Hospices, built in 1443 by a tax collector for the king who, local legend has it, wanted to make up for some of his harsh tax-collecting practices over the years.
The traditional auction sale dates from 1859 and has been held every third Sunday in November since 1924.
